(l)       Expenses
(i) Property operating expenses
Property  operating  expenses  consist  of  quit  rent,  assessment,  utilities,  property  management  fee,  
property  management  reimbursement,  advertising  and  promotion,  maintenance  and  other  property  
outgoings in relation to investment properties where such expenses are the responsibility of the Group 
or the Trust and are recognised on an accrual basis in the year in which they are incurred.
(ii) Manager’s management fee
Manager’s management fee is recognised on an accrual basis using the applicable formula as set out in 
Note 14.
(iii) Trustee’s fee
Trustee’s fee is recognised on an accrual basis using the applicable formula as set out in Note 15.
(iv) Finance costs
Finance costs comprise mainly of interest expense on borrowings and amortisation of transaction costs 
on borrowings which are expensed in profit or loss using the effective interest method over the tenure 
of borrowings.
(m) Tax expense
Tax expense comprises current and deferred tax. Current tax and deferred tax are recognised in profit or loss.
Current tax is the expected tax payable or receivable on the taxable income or loss for the year, using tax rates 
enacted  or  substantively  enacted  by  the  end  of  the  reporting  period,  and  any  adjustment  to  tax  payable  or  
receivable in respect of previous financial years.
Deferred tax is recognised using the liability method, providing for temporary differences between the carrying 
amounts of assets and liabilities in the statements of financial position and their tax bases. Deferred tax is not 
recognised for the initial recognition of assets or liabilities in a transaction that is not a business combination 
and that affects neither accounting nor taxable profit or loss. Deferred tax is measured at the tax rates that are 
expected  to  be  applied  to  the  temporary  differences  when  they  reverse,  based  on  the  laws  that  have  been  
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset if there is a legally enforceable right to offset current tax liabilities 
and assets, and they relate to taxes levied by the same tax authority on the same taxable entity.
A deferred tax asset is recognised to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available 
against  which  the  temporary  difference  can  be  utilised.  Deferred  tax  assets  are  reviewed  at  each  reporting  
period and are reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that the related tax benefit will be realised.
Where investment properties are carried at fair value in accordance with the accounting policy set out in Note 
2(d),  the  amount  of  deferred  tax  recognised  is  measured  using  the  tax  rates  that  would  apply  on  the  sale  of  
those assets at their carrying values at the reporting date unless the property is depreciable and is held with the 
objective to consume substantially all the economic benefits embodied in the property over time, rather than 
through sale. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are not discounted.

(n) Earnings per unit
The Group and the Trust present basic and diluted earnings per unit. Basic earnings per unit is calculated by 
dividing the total return by the weighted-average number of units outstanding during the financial year. Diluted 
earnings per unit is determined by adjusting the total return and the weighted-average number of ordinary units 
outstanding, for the effects of all dilutive potential units.
(o) Operating segments
An  operating  segment  is  a  component  of  the  Group  that  engages  in  business  activities  from  which  it  may  
earn  revenues  and  incur  expenses,  including  revenues  and  expenses  that  relate  to  transactions  with  any  of  
the  Group’s  other  components.  All  operating  segments’  results  are  reviewed  and  used  by  the  Group’s  Chief  
Operating Decision Makers for strategic decision making and resources allocation.
(p) Fair value measurements
Fair  value  of  an  asset  or  a  liability,  except  for  lease  transactions,  is  determined  as  the  price  that  would  be  
received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at 
the measurement date. The measurement assumes that the transaction to sell the asset or transfer the liability 
takes  place  either  in  the  principal  market  or  in  the  absence  of  a  principal  market,  in  the  most  advantageous  
market.
For non-financial asset, the fair value measurement takes into account a market participant’s ability to generate 
economic benefits by using the asset in its highest and best use or by selling it to another market participant 
that would use the asset in its highest and best use.
When measuring the fair value of an asset or a liability, the Group uses observable market data as far as possible. 
Fair value are categorised into different levels in a fair value hierarchy based on the input used in the valuation 
technique as follows:
Level 1:   quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the Group can 
access at the measurement date.
Level 2:  inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, 
either directly or indirectly.
Level 3: unobservable inputs for the asset or liability.
The  Group  recognises  transfers  between  the  levels  of  the  fair  value  hierarchy  as  of  the  date  of  the  event  or

change in circumstances that caused the transfers.

(b) Fair value information
The fair value of investment properties of the Group and of the Trust are categorised as Level 3. The properties 
are valued by independent external valuers using the income capitalisation approach, also known as investment 
approach. This valuation approach takes into account of the gross revenue and outgoings to estimate the net 
income for the properties. Capitalisation rates are then applied to the net income of the investment properties 
to determine the market value of the investment properties.
The  significant  assumptions  and  unobservable  inputs  underlying  the  estimation  of  fair  value  of  investment  
properties  are  those  related  to  term  capitalisation  and  reversionary  capitalisation  rates,  car  park  and  other  
income,  outgoings  expenses  and  allowance  for  void.  Term  capitalisation  and  reversionary  capitalisation  rates  
for the investment properties range from 6.00% to 7.25% (FY2023: 6.00% to 7.25%) and from 6.25% to 7.50% 
(FY2023: 6.25% to 7.50%) respectively. The estimated fair value would increase (decrease) if the capitalisation 
rates, outgoings and allowance for void were lower (higher) and if car park and other income was higher (lower).
(c) Valuation processes applied to the Group and the Trust for Level 3 fair value
The  fair  value  of  investment  properties  is  determined  by  independent  external  valuers  having  appropriate  
recognised  professional  qualifications  and  recent  experience  in  the  location  and  category  of  the  investment  
properties  being  valued.  The  fair  value  of  the  Group’s  and  of  the  Trust’s  investment  property  portfolio  are  
revalued at least every twelve months.

(b) Secured Medium Term Notes Programme
The  Group  has  a  secured  Medium  Term  Notes  Programme  of  up  to  RM3.0  billion  in  nominal  value  (MTN  
Programme) under CLMT MTN Berhad (the Issuer), pursuant to which rated/unrated notes in series or tranches 
may be issued from time to time in Ringgit Malaysia. The MTN Programme has a tenure of twenty years from 
the date of first issuance of MTN, which was on 20 December 2012. The net proceeds from the issue of the MTN 
(after deducting issue expenses) will be on-lent to CLMT, which in turn will utilise such proceeds to refinance 
its  existing  and/or  future  borrowings  and/or  to  finance  investments,  capital  expenditure,  asset  enhancement  
initiatives  and/or  working  capital  of  CLMT.  The  Issuer  will  also  be  allowed  to  use  the  proceeds  to  refinance  
maturing  MTN  on  the  respective  maturity  dates.  The  security  trustee  of  the  MTN  Programme  is  Malaysian  
Trustees Berhad.
On 20 June 2023, the Issuer issued three tranches of RM100.0 million each of unrated and secured MTN (4-
TM) which will be maturing on 20 June 2026, 20 June 2027 and 20 June 2028 respectively. The three tranches 
of 4-TM bear coupon rates of 4.36%, 4.44% and 4.44% per annum respectively for the first two years which is 
payable semi-annually. Upon expiration of the first two years, the Issuer may elect to refix 4-TM with another 
fixed rate.

23.3 Financial risk management
Financial  risk  management  is  integral  to  the  whole  business  of  the  Group  and  of  the  Trust.  The  Group  and  the  Trust  
adopt an integrated approach to manage the financial risks arising in the normal course of business.
The Group and the Trust have identified the following financial risk exposure from its use of financial instruments:
• Liquidity risk
• Credit risk
• Market risk
The Group and the Trust have implemented risk management policies and guidelines which set its tolerance of risk and 
its general risk management philosophy.
23.4 Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is defined as the risk that the Group and the Trust will not be able to meet its financial obligations as they 
fall due.
The Group’s and the Trust’s exposures to liquidity risk arise primarily from various payables and borrowings. The Group 
and the Trust maintain sufficient liquid reserves in terms of cash and credit facilities to ensure, as far as possible, that 
they will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they fall due. In addition, the Manager diligently monitors and 
observes financing covenants to ensure compliance.
The health and sentiments of the debt markets in Malaysia directly affects the liquidity position of the Group and the 
Trust as external sources of funding are needed to fund new acquisitions or asset enhancement initiatives besides the 
need to refinance the existing borrowings when they mature.
At  the  reporting  date,  RM185,126,000  (FY2023:  RM187,787,000)  of  outstanding  revolving  credits  will  be  subject  to  
annual review within the next twelve months. The Group and the Trust will continue to manage their capital structure 
proactively by spreading out the debt maturities to a manageable size and maintaining an optimal gearing level.
It is not expected that the cash flows included in the maturity analysis could occur significantly earlier, or at significantly 
different amounts.

23.5 Credit risk
Credit  risk  is  defined  as  the  risk  of  a  financial  loss  to  the  Group  and  to  the  Trust  if  a  customer  or  counterparty  to  a  
financial instrument fails to meet its contractual obligations. The Group’s and the Trust’s exposures to credit risk arise 
primarily from their trade and other receivables.
Credit risk is controlled by credit verification procedures before lease agreements are entered into with tenants and 
ongoing balance monitoring to ensure minimum credit risk exposure. In addition, there is a stringent collection policy 
in place to ensure that credit risk is minimised. Other than the collection of security deposits, which typically amounts 
to  an  average  of  three  months’  rent  in  the  form  of  cash  or  bankers’  guarantee,  the  Group  and  the  Trust  also  have  
vigilant monitoring and debt collection procedures. Additionally, certain revenue streams such as car park income and 
recovery from tenants do not have credit terms since they are settled on cash or prepayment terms. Debtors turnover 
days of the Group for the financial year was approximately 11 days (FY2023: 14 days).
For other financial assets, the Group and the Trust minimise credit risk by dealing with restricted counterparties that 
meet the appropriate credit criteria and have high credit standing.
The  Manager  establishes  an  allowance  for  impairment  that  represents  its  estimate  of  incurred  losses  in  respect  of  
trade  and  other  receivables.  The  main  component  of  this  allowance  is  a  specific  loss  component  that  relates  to  the  
individually  significant  exposure.  The  allowance  account  in  respect  of  trade  and  other  receivables  is  used  to  record  
impairment losses unless the Manager is satisfied that no recovery of the amount owing is possible. At that point, the 
financial asset is considered irrecoverable and the amount charged to the allowance account is written off against the 
carrying amount of the impaired financial asset.
At the end of financial year, there was no significant concentration of credit risk.
Cash and bank balances are placed with financial institutions which are regulated.
23.6 Market risk
Market risk is the risk that changes in market prices, such as foreign exchange rates, interest rates and other prices that 
will affect the Group’s and the Trust’s financial positions or cash flows.
23.6.1 Interest rate risk
The  Group’s  and  the  Trust’s  investments  in  financial  products  and  its  fixed  rate  borrowings  are  exposed  to  a  
risk of change in the fair values of the instruments due to changes in interest rates. The Group’s and the Trust’s 
floating rate borrowings are exposed to a risk of change in cash flows due to changes in interest rate. Short term 
receivables and payables are not significantly exposed to interest rate risk. Of these instruments, the primary 
interest rate risk exposure of the Group and of the Trust relates to interest-bearing borrowings.
In line with the Group’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Manager adopts a proactive interest 
rate management policy to manage the risk associated with changes in interest rates on the Group’s and the 
Trust’s loan facilities (including borrowing from subsidiary) and also seeking to ensure a competitive level of cost 
of debt. Interest rate risk is managed on an ongoing basis with the primary objective of limiting the extent to 
which interest expense could be affected by adverse movements in interest rates.
To mitigate the Group’s exposure to fluctuation in interest rates, the Manager has locked in a proportion of the 
Group’s and the Trust’s borrowings at fixed interest rates. As at 31 December 2024, the Group’s and the Trust’s 
borrowings at fixed rates are 85.0% (FY2023: 85.3%) while the remaining balances are on floating rates.
The investments in financial products are mainly short-term in nature and not held for trading or speculative 
purposes but are mainly placed in as deposits with licensed banks which yield better returns than cash at bank.

24. CAPITAL MANAGEMENT
The Group’s objectives when managing capital are to maintain a strong capital base so as to maintain investor, creditor 
and market confidence and to ensure optimal returns to unitholders, while maintaining flexibility in respect of future 
capital expenditure and acquisitions. The Manager continues to rigorously monitor the cash position and borrowings of 
the Group with the view of strengthening its capital structure and competitive position.
The Manager maintains an optimal gearing ratio, which is defined as total borrowings divided by total asset value, that 
complies with regulatory requirements and financing covenants. Under the SC’s REIT Guidelines, the gearing ratio of the 
Group should not exceed 50.0% at the time the borrowings or financing facilities or deferred payment arrangements 
are incurred. As at 31 December 2024, the gearing level of the Group stood at 41.3% (FY2023: 42.4%) and has maintained 
the gearing ratio below the statutory threshold during the financial year.

Auditing. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditors’ Responsibilities for the Audit of the

Independence and Other Ethical Responsibilities

Key Audit Matters
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgement, were of most significance in our audit of the financial

the financial statements as a whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not provide a separate opinion on these

Valuation of investment properties
Refer to Note 2(d) – Material accounting policy: Investment properties and Note 4 – Investment properties.
The key audit matter
The  Group  and  the  Trust  own  a  portfolio  of  investment  properties  comprising  shopping  malls  and  logistics  assets  located  
in Malaysia. Investment properties represent the single largest category of assets on the statements of financial position, at 
RM5,130,600,000 and RM5,128,252,000 of the Group and the Trust respectively as at 31 December 2024.
These investment properties are stated at their fair values based on independent external valuations.
The valuation process involves significant judgement in determining the appropriate valuation methodology to be used, and in 
estimating the underlying assumptions to be applied. The valuations are highly sensitive to key assumptions applied such as 
the capitalisation rates i.e. a small change in the assumptions can have a significant impact to the valuation.
This is a key audit matter because of the inherently subjective nature of investment property valuations arising from the use of 
assumptions in the valuation methodology and the financial significance of those balances to the Group and the Trust.

How the matter was addressed in our audit
We performed the following audit procedures, among others:
• We obtained an understanding of the management’s process for reviewing the work of the independent valuers and 
evaluate the design and implementation of the relevant controls.
• We evaluated the qualifications, competency, independence and objectivity of the external valuers.
• We obtained an understanding of the methodology adopted by the external valuers in estimating the fair value of the 
investment properties and assessed whether such methodology is consistent with those used in the industry.
• We interviewed the external valuers to understand their processes, judgements and observations in determining the 
property related data used as input and assumptions applied in their valuations.
• We evaluated the reasonableness of the capitalisation rates used in the valuation by involving our internal specialist.
•  We  tested  data  used  in  the  valuation,  on  a  sample  basis  to  the  underlying  lease  agreements  and  other  supporting  
documents.
•  We  evaluated  the  adequacy  of  the  disclosures  in  the  financial  statements,  in  describing  the  inherent  degree  of  
subjectivity and key assumptions in the estimates.

1.0 GENERAL MARKET OUTLOOK
Macroeconomic & Demographic Overview
The  Malaysian  economy  exhibited  resilience  in  Q3/2024,  
achieving  a  gross  domestic  product  growth  rate  of  5.3%  
compared  to  3.1%  in  the  corresponding  quarter  of  2023.  
This   growth   was   driven   by   strong   domestic   recovery,

prudent fiscal and monetary policies, increased exports and 
investments,  tourism  rebounds,  and  targeted  government  
initiatives.   Household   spending   was   bolstered   by   the   
Employees  Provident  Fund’s  Flexible  Account  (Account  3),  
where it was reported that almost RM10.78 billion has been 
withdrawn as of end-September 2024.
The unemployment rate improved from 3.4% in September 
2023  to  3.2%  in  September  2024,  marking  the  lowest  level  
since COVID-19. This was driven by robust labour demand, 
which  hit  a  6-year  high  of  9.01  million  jobs  in  Q3/2024.  
Employment   growth   was   broad-based,   particularly   in   
services and manufacturing. In terms of demographics, the 
country’s  population  increased  by  2.1%  from  33.4  million  in  
the previous year to 34.1 million.
Inflation remained moderate in 2024, with headline and core 
inflation  averaging  1.8%  in  November  2024.  The  Consumer  
Price Index rose to 133.3 index points in November 2024, a 1.8% 
year-on-year  (YoY)  increase.  Diesel  price  adjustment  had  
minimal impact on inflation, reflecting effective government 
measures  to  contain  cost  pressures.  The  Overnight  Policy  
Rate  was  maintained  at  3.0%  since  May  2023  to  balance  
growth,  inflation  control,  and  financial  stability  amid  global  
uncertainties. By maintaining neutral monetary stance, Bank 
Negara  Malaysia  retains  flexibility  to  respond  to  potential  
market shocks while supporting economic resilience.
In terms of the performance and trend of Malaysia’s industrial 
sector, the Industrial Production Index increased by 3.6% in 
November  2024,  reaching  136.5  index  points.  This  positive  
performance  was  driven  by  strong  manufacturing  output  
in  export-oriented  sectors  –  electrical  and  electronics,  
machinery and equipment, and petroleum products – and 
sustained energy demand. In general, on a YoY comparison 
basis, the manufacturing sector increased by 4.6%, while the 
electricity sector increased by 3.9%. On the other hand, the 
mining  sector  experienced  a  shrink  of  -0.8%  compared  to  
October 2023 performance.
The  property  market  in  Malaysia  has  shown  consistent  
growth   and   resilience   in   2024,   as   evidenced   by   the   
remarkable 14.4% YoY increase in transaction value, reaching 
RM163.0   billion   as   of   September   2024.   Supported   by   
government  incentives  and  strong  economic  conditions  
that are intended to stimulate the real estate industry, this 
total  transaction  value  represents  the  best  performance  
over the past five years.
In the 2025 Budget, the government has outlined substantial 
allocations   for   projects   under   the   MADANI   Economy   
framework, including initiatives to enhance productivity and 
foster  innovation.  Notably,  investments  are  anticipated  in  
high-value  industries  like  electronics  and  electrical  (E&E),  
which  are  expected  to  recover  from  global  technological  
advancements,    with    investments    aimed    at    boosting    
manufacturing capabilities and export potential.
To support the industrial sector, the government introduced 
the   New   Investment   Incentives   Framework.   Under   this   
framework,   RM1   billion   has   been   allocated   to   attract   
high-value  foreign  investments,  particularly  in  advanced  
manufacturing and technology sectors. Furthermore, Supply 
Chain  Resilience  Initiatives  include  double  tax  deductions  
for multinational enterprises (MNEs) on eligible supply chain 
resilience  expenses,  capped  at  RM2  million  per  year  for  
three  consecutive  years;  tax  deductions  on  investments  
for MNEs and their suppliers engaging in joint ventures with 
local  vendors,  and  a  RM100  million  matching  investment  
fund to develop local suppliers in sectors like E&E, specialty 
chemicals, and medical devices.
For the retail sector, the expansion of the Sales and Service 
Tax (SST) will take effect on May 1, 2025. The SST framework 
will be broadened to include non-essential food items and 
certain  commercial  services,  such  as  fee-based  financial  
services.  This  aims  to  create  a  more  equitable  tax  system

and   support   long-term   fiscal   sustainability.   Meanwhile,   
consumer-centric  measures  are  set  to  uplift  household  
income  through  initiatives  such  as  higher  minimum  wages  
and  increased  cash  handouts  for  lower-income  groups.  
These   measures   are   expected   to   stimulate   consumer   
spending, benefiting the retail sector.

2.0 RETAIL MARKET OVERVIEW & TRENDS
The  global  retail  landscape  is  rapidly  evolving,  driven  by

the  growth  of  e-commerce,  advancements  in  technology  
and  shifting  consumer  expectations.  New  malls  and  retail  
destinations  that  opened  in  2024,  including  Bloomsvale  
Shopping  Gallery,  Elmina  Lakeside  Mall,  168  Park  Mall  and  
New  Ocean  Fine  Food  City  in  Greater  Kuala  Lumpur,  along  
with  Sunshine  Mall  @  Sunshine  Central  in  Penang,  have  
redefined  the  traditional  retail  concept,  offering  a  fresh  
and  innovative  experience.  Consumer  preferences  have  
evolved  since  the  pandemic,  with  shoppers  now  seeking  
more  than  just  transactional  retail  but  experiential  retail  
experience which attracts foot traffic and improves shopper 
experience.   By   offering   enhanced   experimental   retail   
experiences, businesses can create more engaging shopping 
environments.   This   encourages   repeat   customer   visits,   
driving demand for more frequent in-store interactions and 
demonstrating  the  continued  relevance  of  physical  retail.  
Some  of  the  offerings  include  indoor  theme  parks,  virtual  
reality  (VR)  gaming  center  and  sports  attractions  such  as  
rock climbing gyms like Camp5 at Sungei Wang Plaza, Batuu 
Climbing  at  3  Damansara,  Project  Rock  Climbing  Gym  at  
Gurney Plaza and Rocky Basecamp at AEON Mall Shah Alam, 
pickleball courts at Ultra Sports Center at 168 Park Mall and 
Arena  A.T.A.S  at  SACC  Mall,  paddleball  courts  at  ASCARO  
Padel  &  Social  Club  at  1  Utama,  PadelKu  at  Berjaya  Times  
Square,  futsal  courts  at  Padang@1  Utama  and  IOI  Sports  
Centre at IOI City Mall Putrajaya and ice skating rinks include 
Blue Ice Snow Park at Pavilion Bukit Jalil and Blue Ice Skating 
Rink  at  KL  East  Mall.  Indoor  theme  parks  include  Escape  
Park  at  Paradigm  Mall  Petaling  Jaya,  Game  On  Sports  Hub  
at  1  Utama,  Pavilion  Bukit  Jalil  and  KSL  Esplanade  Mall  and  
SuperPark  at  Avenue  K  Shopping  Mall.  VR  gaming  center  
includes VAR Live MY at MyTOWN Shopping Centre, Virtual 
Reality Center at KL East Mall and VR Funn at 1 Utama, which 
could  provide  interactive  elements  that  enhance  visitor  
experiences and attract a diverse range of shoppers.
In  addition  to  experiential  retail,  key  trends  shaping  the  
market   include   omnichannel   retail,   where   physical   and   
digital  shopping  experiences  are  seamlessly  integrated.  
Technological   advancements   are   also   transforming   the   
retail  experience,  with  innovations  such  as  smart  trolleys  
introduced by Jaya Grocer and AEON, whilst Harvey Norman 
has also introduced bedMATCH®, an exclusive Smart Sleep 
Technology  powered  by  AI,  the  first  of  its  kind  in  Malaysia,  
which analyses body profiles and sleeping habits to provide 
personalised mattress recommendations.
Retail Market Outlook
In  2024,  Malaysia’s  retail  sector  experienced  early-year  
growth with a 7.8% YoY increase, driven by festive spending 
during the Chinese New Year and school holidays. However, 
growth slowed to 0.6% YoY in Q2/2024 attributed to several 
factors,   including   rising   costs,   particularly   in   food   and   
beverages  (F&B)  due  to  increased  material  costs,  such  as  
dairy products, and the increase of SST from 6% to 8%, which 
took effect in March 2024. Retail sales improved in Q3/2024, 
growing  3.8%  YoY,  led  by  the  minimarket  and  convenience  
store  subsector,  with  Q4/2024  expected  to  see  a  4.4%  
YoY  growth,  supported  by  steady  shopper  traffic.  In  terms  
of  annual  performance,  Retail  Group  Malaysia  (RGM)  has  
forecasted an overall growth of 3.9% for full year 2024.
Looking  ahead  to  2025,  the  retail  sector  is  forecasted  to  
grow steadily, with RGM projecting a 4.0% growth, supported 
by  government  initiatives  such  as  higher  minimum  wages  
and subsidies in Budget 2025, which are expected to boost 
purchasing   power   and   stimulate   private   consumption.   
However, challenges remain, with policy measures, including 
subsidy   rationalisation   for   RON95   petrol   by   mid-2025   
and  higher  excise  duties  on  sugar-sweetened  beverages,  
which  may  impact  consumer  spending.  The  rise  in  fuel  
costs  could  also  elevate  operational  and  transportations  
cost, prompting retailers to reassess pricing strategies and

optimise their supply chain. Additionally, shifting consumer 
behaviours  and  the  continued  growth  of  online  shopping  
will  put  pressure  on  physical  stores,  making  omnichannel  
strategies increasingly essential. Global trends, such as the 
ongoing boycott of certain international franchises, may also 
affect  global  operations  and  consumer  sentiment,  adding  
complexity to the retail landscape.

3.0    INDUSTRIAL    AND    LOGISTICS    MARKET    
OVERVIEW & TRENDS
The    industrial    sector    in    Malaysia    witnessed    strong    
performance  and  rising  investment  in  2024.  The  positive  
performance of the Malaysian economy can be associated 
with a steady recovery in exports and household spending, 
which   is   bolstered   by   ongoing   growth   in   employment   
and  wages.  Malaysia’s  position  as  a  strategic  investment  
destination  has  led  to  significant  expansion  in  investment  
activities.   As   reported   by   MIDA,   the   total   approved   
investment  in  9M/2024  has  recorded  an  improvement  of  
10.7%  as  compared  to  the  same  period  in  2023  (RM254.7

billion,   9M/2024;   RM230.2   billion,   9M/2023).   Domestic   
investment  constituted  the  predominant  share  of  total  
capital investment, contributing 58.1% to the overall figure. In 
9M/2024, domestic investment attained a value of RM148.0 
billion, signifying a substantial 44.2% increase relative to the 
corresponding period in 2023 (RM102.7 billion, 9M/2023). In 
contrast,  foreign  investment  registered  a  decline  of  16.3%  
in  9M/2024,  reaching  RM106.7  billion  compared  to  RM127.5  
billion  in  the  same  period  in  2023.  The  top  five  states  that  
took  the  lion’s  share  of  investments,  amounting  to  80.6%  
of  the  total  approved  investments,  are  Selangor  (RM66.8

billion),    Wilayah    Persekutuan    Kuala    Lumpur    (RM63.9    
billion),   Kedah   (RM34.0   billion),   Pulau   Pinang   (RM22.6   
billion) and Johor (RM18.1 billion). The manufacturing sector 
plays  a  crucial  role  in  driving  the  country’s  investments  
by  attracting  a  substantial  share  of  both  domestic  and  
foreign  direct  investments  (FDI),  owing  to  its  importance  
in producing goods for export and domestic consumption. 
As  of  9M/2024,  this  sector  accounted  for  34.9%  of  the  
total  approved  investments,  amounting  to  RM88.8  billion.  
Electrical   and   electronics   (E&E)   contributed   the   most   
to  the  manufacturing  sector  with  an  investment  value  
of  RM47.0  billion,  followed  by  chemicals  and  chemicals  
products (RM7.0 billion), transport equipment (RM7.0 billion), 
machinery and equipment (RM6.3 billion), and non-metallic 
mineral products (RM4.2 billion).
Malaysia  is  on  track  to  becoming  Asia’s  third-largest  Data  
Centre  market  after  Japan  and  India,  driven  by  significant  
market  expansion,  mainly  in  Iskandar  Malaysia  and  Greater  
KL.   In   2024,   Malaysia   secured   approximately   RM141.72   
billion  in  digital  investment  within  the  first  ten  months,  a  
significant  threefold  increase  compared  to  the  RM46.2  
billion achieved in the entirety of 2023. This surge in digital 
investment  was  fueled  by  substantial  commitments  from  
major tech giants, including Google, Amazon Web Services, 
Microsoft,  ByteDance,  and  Oracle.  According  to  the  SEA-5  
Data  Center  Opportunity  Index,  Malaysia  has  maintained  
its  leading  position,  securing  a  committed  annual  take-up  
of  429  megawatts  (MW),  surpassing  regional  competitors  
like Indonesia and Thailand. The strong demand is driven by 
increased  demand  from  telecommunications  and  internet  
service  providers,  coupled  with  the  expansion  of  Internet  
of  Things  (IoT),  robust  global  network  connectivity  and  the  
widespread adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as well as 
the  IoT-enabled  digital  solutions.  Industrial  hotspot  such  
as  Iskandar  Malaysia  and  Greater  KL  continue  to  attract  
the  highest  concentration  of  Data  Center  investments.  
Additionally,    the    Malaysian    government    has    recently    
approved  the  Data  Centre  Planning  Guidelines  (GPP)  to  
standardise  and  streamline  the  application  and  planning  
approval  processes,  enhancing  business  efficiency  and  
strengthening the Data Centre ecosystem in the nation.
Industrial Market Outlook
Malaysia’s industrial sector is expected to continue flourish 
in   2025,   fueled   by   Malaysian   government’s   proactive   
measures  and  focus  on  high-value  manufacturing  sector  
have   attracted   significant   interest   from   investors.   The   
recent  Malaysia’s  Budget  2025  incentives  is  anticipated  
to  significantly  impact  high-value  manufacturing  sectors,  
including   EVs,   semiconductors   and   aerospace   related   
sectors, through initiatives that could drive high-skilled job 
creation and accelerate technological advancements.
As    technology    advances,    the    need    for    high-grade    
warehouses/facilities   will   continue   to   grow.   The   Smart   
Logistics Complex tax incentive was introduced in Malaysia’s 
Budget 2025 to enhance the supply chain efficiency through 
the  adoption  of  advance  technologies  such  as  AI,  Internet

of Things (IoT) and blockchain into logistics operations. The 
qualified companies can claim for Investment Tax Allowance 
(ITA)  of  60%  on  eligible  Capital  Expenditure  (CAPEX)  over  
a  period  of  5  years  which  can  be  applied  against  up  to  
70%  of  the  company’s  statutory  income  for  each  year  of  
assessment.  This  incentive  promotes  the  development  of  
advanced automation and modern warehouse facilities while 
enhancing competitiveness and fostering trade activities. To 
maintain competitiveness and generate positive investment 
yields,  existing  conventional  warehouses  must  undergo  
upgrades  to  incorporate  modern  features  and  capabilities.  
This will ensure they remain competitive with the advanced 
warehouses  currently  available  in  the  market  within  the  
evolving logistics landscape.
The industrial sector has demonstrated resilience throughout 
the pandemic, driven by the surge in e-commerce and the 
accelerating  demand  for  warehouse  and  logistics  space.  
The  booming  e-commerce  industry  has  been  a  significant  
contributor  to  rental  appreciation  in  recent  years.  Due  to  
robust  demand,  warehouses  located  in  prime  logistics  
regions such as Greater Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Iskandar 
Malaysia   have   consistently   experienced   stable   rental   
growth throughout the year. The sustained growth in online 
retail, coupled with stable e-commerce market penetration 
and  the  rolled  out  of  favorable  government  policies,  is  
expected to maintain the stability of rental rates despite the 
anticipated increase in the supply of industrial space in the 
near future.

The   industrial   market   remained   robust   in   Greater   KL   
throughout 2024, with 10 major deals amounting to RM1.30 
billion,  indicating  continued  investor  interest  in  the  sector.  
Klang recorded the highest number of transactions, totalling 
12 and valued at RM0.74 billion, accounting for 37% of Greater 
KL’s total transaction value. Based on our observation, 46% of 
industrial transactions worth RM334.6 million were acquired 
for  own  usage.  The  recent  Budget  2025  has  unveiled  an  
allocation  of  RM107  million  for  constructing  and  upgrading  
roads along the Pulau Indah Ring Road and North Port Klang. 
This is expected to further stimulate the performance of the 
logistics sector.
The  surge  in  e-commerce  and  the  escalating  demand  for  
efficient  warehouse  operations  have  spurred  the  adoption

of   Automated   Storage   and   Retrieval   Systems   (ASRS)   
solutions.  Logistics  players  are  increasingly  transitioning  
to  ASRS  systems  to  optimise  storage  capacity,  reduce  
labor costs and enhance overall operational efficiency. This 
trend  is  particularly  evident  in  the  Greater  Kuala  Lumpur  
region, where developers are actively investing in advanced 
warehousing   technologies   to   maintain   competitiveness.   
Tasco’s newly under construction warehouses in Northport 
will   incorporate   ASRS   systems   within   their   upcoming   
600,000  sq  ft  cold  storage  facility.  The  newly  completed  
3-storey  Omega  Bukit  Raja  smart  warehouse  in  Bandar  
Bukit   Raja   has   been   integrated   with   ASRS,   capable   of   
accommodating 100,000 pallets.
CLMT recently acquired an ASRS property in Elmina Business 
Park, at a consideration of RM180 million. Upon completion, 
the  property  will  be  leased  to  Projek  Tetap  Teguh  Sdn  Bhd  
for a 10-year term. Given the competitive market demands 
of   industrial   occupiers   and   the   evolving   landscape   of   
the  industrial  sector,  the  demand  for  high-specification  
warehouses has significantly increased.
With  the  current  shift  in  industry  trends,  developers  are  
increasingly   investing   in   high-quality   logistics   facilities   
with  some  investors  seen  to  be  actively  investing  in  asset  
enhancement initiatives (AEI) for its warehouse portfolio to 
remain competitive in terms of value and performance. Our 
analysis  of  established  Malaysian  REITs  reveals  a  positive  
leasing   market   trend,   with   the   samplings   of   industrial   
warehouses  demonstrating  a  strong  98%  occupancy  rate.  
The recent completion of several significant developments 
such  as  Mapletree  Logistics  Hub-Jubli  Perak  (Shah  Alam),  
Maersk  Warehouse  (Shah  Alam),  Bukit  Raja  International  
Industrial Complex (BRIIC) by YTL (Klang), E-Metro Logistics 
Park – MetroHub 2 (Klang) and OMEGA 1 (Klang) have added 
a  substantial  6.4  million  square  feet  of  warehousing  space,  
primarily in Shah Alam and Klang.

E-Metro Logistics Park, Metrohub 1, and Metrohub 2 reported

15-year master lease agreement. ALP is a 30% shareholder 
in  the  joint  venture,  with  the  remaining  70%  held  by  the

opportunity for the growing demand for warehousing space 
in  Greater  KL.  With  the  optimistic  growth  of  e-commerce  
market  moving  forward,  the  influx  of  warehousing/logistics  
space could provide logistics players with greater options for 
their operational needs, supporting overall market vibrancy. 
However,  as  businesses  increasingly  consolidate  smaller  
spaces into larger, integrated warehouses of higher quality, 
this will drive demand for these new incoming supply.
There are three major upcoming industrial parks announced 
in the year mainly focusing on the southern region focusing 
in Sepang and Banting area which include MSS Business Park 
by Mah Sing in Sepang, IOI Industrial Park by IOI in Banting and 
A-Park  Bangi  by  Ancubic  in  Bangi.  All  these  developments  
bring a total of 469 acres development area in total. Besides, 
there is also an upcoming park announced by a joint venture 
between AME and KLK located in Kuala Selangor.
There  are  a  limited  number  of  prominent  parks  offering  
ready-built  factories.  Elmina  Business  Park  by  Sime  Darby  
and Eco Business Park V by EcoWorld are notable examples. 
Sime   Darby   Property   Bhd’s   Signature   Collection   Twin   
Factories  within  Elmina  Business  Park  Stage  2  experienced  
100%   occupancy   upon   launch,   signifying   the   growing   
demand for well-planned industrial spaces in the Greater KL. 
The  development  encompasses  26.2  acres  and  comprises

60 semi-detached factory units available in two sizes: Type 
A  (65’  x  142’,  4,410  sq.  ft.)  priced  from  RM3.68  million  and  
Type B (80’ x 200’, 9,573 sq. ft.) starting from RM5.98 million. 
In  Q1/2024,  Eco  Business  Park  V  successfully  disposed  of  
its industrial developments, including cluster factories (five 
units),  industrial  plots  (five  plots),  and  a  single  Built-to-Suit  
unit,  to  eleven  distinct  companies.  Since  its  launch  in  2017,  
EBP V has achieved complete take-up for the West, North, 
and  Central  Gates,  with  the  fully  completed  East  Gate  
exceeding 90% occupancy.
Furthermore, we observe a growing trend among developers 
to  venture  into  the  development  of  Centralised  Labour  
Quarters (CLQs) in Greater KL.
•  Titijaya  Land  Berhad  has  signed  a  Memorandum  of  
Understanding  (MoU)  with  PMB  Aluminium  Sdn  Bhd  to  
co-develop  HALO,  a  10-storey  purpose-built  CLQ  in  
Klang  Sentral,  with  a  capacity  to  accommodate  3,000  
workers.
•  Unitrade  Industries  Bhd  has  also  acquired  land  for  the  
development  of  seven  blocks  of  three-storey  modular  
houses with an approximate built-up area of 67,611 sq. ft 
in Sungai Buloh.
The Malaysia Semiconductor IC Design Park in Puchong is the 
nation’s  first  chip  design  hub,  spanning  across  60,000  sq.  
ft. in area. The park houses anchor tenants like Maistorage, 
Skyechip,    Weeroc,    AppAsia    ChipsBank,    SensoremTek    
Sdn  Bhd  etc.  Due  to  its  full  occupancy,  the  Selangor  state  
government is considering developing a second chip design 
park  in  Cyberjaya  in  2025,  which  may  be  similar  in  size  or  
larger than the Puchong site.
The establishment of this park aligns with the government’s 
initiative   to   strengthen   the   Malaysian   semiconductor   
ecosystem.   This   initiative   encompasses   both   upstream   
and  downstream  sectors,  focus  on  leveraging  the  existing  
base of Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) in the state. 
This initiative aims to position Malaysia at the higher end of 
the semiconductor manufacturing value chain by fostering 
a  strong  IC  design  ecosystem.  This  strategy  leverages  the  
current  global  competition  for  semiconductor  dominance  
(“chip war”) to attract and nurture local talent and innovation. 
This   platform   will   effectively   complement   the   existing   
semiconductor industries within the Greater Kuala Lumpur 
region and facilitate the absorption of spillover effects from 
the thriving Electronics and Electrical (E&E) sector in Penang.

As  of  9M/2024,  Penang  ranks  among  the  top  five  states  
contributing to Malaysia’s investment, securing over RM22.6 
billion in approved investments, driven by the ongoing trade 
tension between China and US, benefiting the electrical and 
electronics (E&E) industry. This has driven global companies 
to diversify their manufacturing hub locations out of China,

align with the “China Plus One” strategy, with major players 
such as Intel, Swisslog and Boston Scientific Corporation has 
seen expanding their footprint in Penang.
The  Penang  government  is  actively  promoting  IC  Design,  
capitalizing   on   the   state’s   existing   strengths   in   the   
Electrical   and   Electronic   (E&E)   industry,   including   its   
robust   infrastructure   and   established   ecosystem   as   a   
semiconductor   hub.   The   state   is   strategically   shifting   
towards   front-end   activities,   encouraging   local   players   
to  ascend  the  value  chain  by  engaging  in  IC  Design.  The  
launch  of  'Penang  Silicon  Design  @5km+'  is  a  pivotal  step  
in  advancing  the  semiconductor  industry,  aligning  with  
the  National  Semiconductor  Strategy  (NSS).  This  initiative  
leverages  the  existing  strengths  of  the  local  industry,  with  
a  particular  focus  on  power  chips  and  chip  design.  Key  
components  of  'Penang  Silicon  Design  @5km+'  include  the  
Penang  IC  Design  &  Digital  Park@Bayan  Lepas,  the  Penang  
Chip Design Academy @Penang Skills Development Centre 
(PSDC),  and  the  Silicon  Research  and  Incubation  Space  
@GBS  TechSpace.  These  initiatives  collectively  foster  a  
comprehensive  IC  design  ecosystem.  This  collaborative  
approach   facilitates   interaction   between   government,   
academia,  and  industry  players,  driving  the  growth  of  the  
IC  design  ecosystem  in  Penang.  Globetronics  Technology  
Bhd  will  collaborate  with  Invest  Penang  to  strengthen  the  
semiconductor and IC design ecosystem. As an outsourced 
semiconductor    assembly    and    test    (OSAT)    provider,    
Globetronics  will  support  chip  design  houses  by  offering  
expertise  in  package  design  and  process  development,  as  
well as providing assembly, test, engineering sample builds, 
and qualification builds.
The  Silicon  Island  project  is  a  2,300-acre  land  reclamation  
initiative in Penang, forming part of the larger Penang South 
Islands  (PSI)  master  plan.  Within  this  project,  a  700-acre  
Green  Tech  Park  is  dedicated  to  industrial  development  
which  is  expected  to  commence  operation  by  2027.  The  
entire  park  is  fully  covered  by  renewable  energy,  dual-
purpose  sewage  treatment  plant  as  well  as  high  speed  
digital  connectivity  and  smart  security.  Some  of  the  major  
promoted    industry    include    among    others    advanced    
packaging,    semiconductor    IC,    software    campus    and    
design, medical devices, product design and development, 
automated  test  equipment  and  equipment  fabrication  as  
well as embedded system design. The first phase of Silicon 
Island is expected to be completed by 2032.
Furthermore,  the  Penang  government  is  undertaking  the  
expansion of Penang International Airport (PIA). This project 
aims  to  increase  the  airport’s  annual  passenger  capacity  
by  12  million,  with  a  total  investment  of  RM1.55  billion.  The  
scope  of  work  includes  support  building  construction,  a  
remote digital virtual tower, airside and apron infrastructure 
improvements, and the main terminal. Once completed, PIA 
will  become  Malaysia’s  second-largest  airport,  boasting  an  
increased aircraft parking capacity of 28 commercial planes.
In  addition,  the  Mutiara  LRT  Line  project  will  stretch  along  
29.5  kilometers,  connecting  21  stations,  including  Bayan  
Lepas, Komtar and Butterworth. The project is expected to 
begin construction by early 2025 and operational by 2030.
The Penang government has unveiled strategic plans to drive 
growth in new areas, particularly focusing on Seberang Prai. 
These plans include initiatives such as increasing plot ratios 
for development projects to match those on Penang Island 
and  enhancing  the  region’s  connectivity  and  accessibility.  
The  development  in  the  northern  region  could  potentially  
benefit  from  the  spillover  effects  of  the  established  E&E  
hub  in  southern  Seberang  Prai,  including  Batu  Kawan,  Bukit

tenant. These developments align with Penang’s initiative to 
establish  a  logistics  hub  in  Seberang  Perai,  supporting  the  
growth of neighbouring technology parks like Bandar Cassia 
and Batu Kawan Industrial Park 3, which cater to electronics, 
semiconductors,  and  automotive  sectors.  Valdor  Industrial  
Park strategically capitalises on the region’s strong industrial 
foundation and proximity to established industrial zones.
Ideal  Business  Hub,  an  industrial  project  by  Ideal  Business  
Group,  was  launched  across  28  acres  of  freehold  land  in  
Penang Technology Park @ Bertam with a gross development 
value (GDV) of RM260 million. The project comprises 88 units 
of ready-built factories, including a mix of detached, semi-
detached, and cluster factories, targeting industrial players 
seeking  modern  industrial  spaces.  Key  features  include  
9.14-meter-high  ceilings  and  a  column-free  design  layout,  
making  it  ideal  for  logistics  and  manufacturing  operators.  
The project is expected to be completed by 2026.
The  Penang  Development  Corporation  (PDC)  has  been  
actively engaged in the development of industrial park within 
the Seberang Prai region, with forthcoming projects such as 
Bandar Cassia Technology Park, Batu Kawan Industrial Park 
3, and Penang Science Park South strategically positioned to 
address the anticipated surge in demand for industrial land, 
particularly  within  the  burgeoning  semiconductor  sector.  
This  proactive  approach  by  PDC  serves  to  augment  the  
availability  of  industrial  options  for  prospective  investors.  
Furthermore,  private  sector  initiatives  are  also  underway,  
Ancubic’s   A-Park   Batu   Kawan,   which   encompasses   50   
ready-built  factory  units,  offering  1.5-storey  and  2-storey  
semi-detached  and  detached  factories,  with  sizes  ranging  
from  6,800  sq  ft  to  16,700  sf  starting  at  RM4  million.  
Notably, the first phase of A-Park Batu Kawan demonstrated 
significant market traction, achieving a commendable 90% 
take-up rate upon its launch in March 2024.
In  addition,  the  Penang  Development  Corporation  (PDC)  is  
also  developing  infrastructures  for  800  acres  of  industrial  
land in East Batu Kawan, expected to be completed in 2028. 
The  ongoing  construction  of  Batu  Kawan  Industrial  Park  lll,  
which  spans  407  acres,  is  also  set  to  complement  existing  
facilities  and  cater  to  more  MNCs  and  local  companies.  
Generally, rental rates for industrial warehouses and logistics 
facilities   remain   stable,   reflecting   positive   investment   
activity and overall market stability within the state.

Johor is set to be Malaysia’s next growth engine, driven by Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) initiative which 
has  positively  impacted  bilateral  investments  and  fostered  regional  development  between  Malaysia  and  Singapore.  The  
scope  of  the  JS-SEZ  has  been  expanded  to  include  four  new  flagship  zones:  Sedenak,  Forest  City,  Pengerang  Integrated  
Petroleum Complex (PIPC) and Desaru, bringing the total number of flagship zones within the JS-SEZ to nine. The primary 
objective of the JS-SEZ is to stimulate economic growth in the region through a combination of attractive incentives and 
strategic  infrastructure  development.  The  initiative  focuses  on  key  sectors  such  as  Aerospace,  Electrical  &  Electronics,  
Chemicals, and Medical Devices & Pharmaceuticals.
SD Guthrie Bhd and AME Industrial Park Sdn Bhd have announced a collaboration to develop a green industrial park within 
the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ). The project will cover a total area of 641 acres focusing on high-value 
industries, including logistics and advanced manufacturing, by offering flexible factory options. The park will also feature a 
dedicated solar park to provide renewable energy for the site.
Besides, Paragon Globe Berhad (PGB) will develop its first green industrial park, PGB TECH PARK @ NUSAJAYA, with a total 
gross development value of RM957 million located in Gerbang Nusajaya. The development will be built on a 116-acre land 
within  the  Johor-Singapore  Special  Economic  Zone  (JS-SEZ)  in  two  phases  which  include  88  factory  units  for  Phase  1,  
completed in 2027, while Phase 2 will feature 8 units of factories and 1 dormitory with 350 rooms to accommodate up to 
5,250 workers and expected to commence in 2026 and be completed in 2028. All these notable developments will create a 
more favorable investment climate within the JS-SEZ, fostering robust industrial growth.

GHG Emissions Data Methodology
ApproachCLMT computes Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions using Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and 
Reporting Standard (2004), and Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting 
and Reporting Standard (2011), unless otherwise stated.
CLMT uses the operational control approach as defined by the GHG Protocol, and determined that it has 
operational control over the properties that CLI-operationally manages.

4
), nitrous oxide (N
2
O),

6

used by CLMT.

Scope 3 GHG

Emissions
Cat 3 Fuel- and energy-related activities
Relates to emissions from the production and transmission and distribution of fuels and energy consumed 
by CLMT, that are not accounted for in Scope 1 and 2. 
Emission and Conversion factors
WTT and transmission and distribution loss emission factors used for computation of emissions were from 
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2024. UK Government GHG Conversion 
Factors for Company Reporting 2021 where country-specific emission factor was unavailable in the 2024 
database. 
Changes in reporting period 
New disclosure category in 2024.
Cat 5 Waste generated in own operations 
Relates to emissions from the disposal of landlord and tenant waste generated at properties. For non-
recycled waste, the waste disposal method is landfill. 
For recycled waste, emissions were computed for recycled paper, metal, plastic, glass, e-waste, food 
waste, and other recycled waste. 
Emission and Conversion factors 
US EPA Emission Factors Hub 2024. 
Changes in reporting period
New disclosure category in 2024.
Cat 6 Business travel (air travel)
Relates to emissions from corporate air travel by CLMT employees based on air travel distance provided 
by air travel agency. 
Emission and Conversion factors
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2024.
Changes in reporting period
New disclosure category in 2024.
Cat 13 Downstream leased assets (Landlord and tenant emissions of owned properties not accounted  
for in Scope 1 and 2) 
Relates to tenant emissions of CLMT-owned and CLI-operationally managed properties, and landlord and 
tenant emissions of CLMT-owned but third-party operationally managed properties.
Emission and Conversion factors 
IEA 2024 v1.1 (AR6 Applied). 
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2024.

Enhanced disclosure of landlord and tenant emissions of CLMT-owned but third-party operationally 
managed properties in 2024.

Ordinary Business
1.  Audited  Financial  Statements  of  CLMT  for  the  financial  year  ended  31  December  2024  together  with  the  
Reports of Trustee, Manager and Auditors thereon
The Audited Financial Statements are laid before the unitholders for discussion only pursuant to Paragraph 13.18(b) 
of the Guidelines on Listed Real Estate Investment Trusts. The Audited Financial Statements do not require a formal 
approval of the unitholders. Hence, this matter will not be put forward for voting.
Special Business
2. Ordinary Resolution 1 – Proposed Authority 1
The Proposed Ordinary Resolution 1, if passed, would enable the Manager to allot and issue New Units from time to 
time provided that the aggregate number of the New Units to be issued during the Validity Period, when aggregated 
with the number of units issued during the preceding 12 months must not exceed 20% of the total number of units 
issued in CLMT for the time being.
The Proposed Authority 1 will allow the Manager the flexibility to allot and issue New Units to raise funds to finance 
future investments, acquisitions and capital expenditure to enhance the value of CLMT and/or to refinance existing 
debt as well as for working capital purposes, subject to the relevant laws and regulations. With the Proposed Authority 
1, delays and further costs involved in convening separate general meetings to approve such issue of New Units to 
raise funds can be avoided. Any allotment and issuance of New Units pursuant to the Proposed Authority 1 will be

subject to the relevant approvals of Securities Commission Malaysia and Bursa Securities.
The Proposed Ordinary Resolution 1 is a renewal of the previous year's mandate. As at the date of this Notice, no New 
Units have been issued pursuant to the mandate granted to the Manager at the previous AGM of CLMT.
3. Ordinary Resolution 2 – Proposed Renewal of Unit Buy-Back Mandate
Unitholders are advised to refer to the Statement to Unitholders dated 6 March 2025, which is available on CLMT’s 
website at www.clmt.com.my for further information.
4. Ordinary Resolution 3 – Proposed Authority 2
The Proposed Authority 2, if passed, will give authority to the Board to allot and issue the DRP New Units pursuant to 
the DRP upon such terms and conditions and to such persons as the Manager may in its absolute discretion deem 
fit and in the best interest of CLMT and its Unitholders, and such authority shall expire at the conclusion of the next 
AGM of CLMT.
CLMT had applied the DRP to the first income distribution for the period from 1 January 2024 to 30 June 2024 (First 
Income Distribution) which was declared on 24 July 2024 and a total of 38,113,249 New Units were issued under the 
First  Income  Distribution  on  20  September  2024.  The  New  Units  issued  under  the  First  Income  Distribution  were  
listed on the Main Market of Bursa Securities on 23 September 2024.
CLMT  had  also  applied  the  DRP  to  the  final  income  distribution  for  the  period  from  1  July  2024  to  31  December  
2024 (Final Income Distribution) which was declared on 22 January 2025. Upon the closing time for submitting the 
distribution reinvestment form on 6 March 2025, the New Units to be issued under the Final Income Distribution will 
be issued on 17 March 2025 and listed on the Main Market of Bursa Securities on 19 March 2025.
